learn.hook: Biscuits made in a factory near Pune reach a tiny shop in Arunachal. In between stands a quiet hero of trade: the wholesaler.
points: Internal trade is the buying and selling of goods and services within the boundaries of a nation. No customs duty or import duty is levied, since goods are produced and sold within the country. It is classified into wholesale trade and retail trade.
Wholesale trade means buying and selling goods in large quantities, usually from manufacturers, and selling them to retailers or other businesses (not to final consumers).

Services of wholesalers to manufacturers: facilitating large-scale production (by buying in bulk); bearing risk (of price fall, theft, spoilage); financial assistance (paying cash for goods, sometimes in advance); expert advice (on consumer preferences and market trends); help in marketing (distributing to many retailers); facilitating continuity of production; storage (warehousing goods until needed).

Services of wholesalers to retailers: availability of goods (ready stock from many producers); marketing support (advertising and promotion); grant of credit; specialised knowledge (about products and demand); risk sharing (retailers buy in small lots, so they carry less stock).

example.q: A wholesaler buys 10,000 packets of tea from a manufacturer each month, stores them and sells to 200 small shops on 15 days' credit. Name one service to the manufacturer and one to the retailers.
steps: Buying in bulk and storing goods helps the manufacturer produce on a large scale continuously.
Selling on 15 days' credit helps retailers: grant of credit.
example.answer: To manufacturer: facilitating large-scale production and storage; to retailers: grant of credit.

learn.reallife: Wholesale mandis like Azadpur in Delhi and Vashi in Navi Mumbai move huge volumes of fruits and vegetables from farmers to thousands of retailers every day.

topics.title: Retail trade and services of retailers

learn.hook: The corner kirana shop knows your family's favourite brand of atta, offers credit until the month-end and introduces new products. It is the final link to the consumer.
points: A retailer is a business enterprise that sells goods and services directly to final consumers for their personal, non-business use, usually in small quantities. Retailing is the last link in the chain of distribution.

Services to manufacturers and wholesalers: help in distribution (making goods available to scattered consumers); personal selling (explaining and persuading); enabling large-scale operations (so producers and wholesalers need not deal with each consumer); collecting market information (about tastes and preferences); help in promotion (displays and in-store promotion).

Services to consumers: regular availability of products; new products information; convenience in buying (small quantities, near homes, long hours); wide selection; after-sales services (delivery, repairs, spare parts); credit facilities to regular buyers.

example.q: A mobile shop owner tells the company that young buyers in his area prefer phones with big batteries. Which service of retailers is this?
steps: He is passing on information about customer preferences to the company.
That is collecting market information.
example.answer: Collecting market information (a service to manufacturers).

learn.hook: The vegetable vendor with a handcart, the weekly haat in a village, the man selling toys outside a railway station: retailers who come to you.
points: Itinerant retailers are traders who do not have a fixed place of business; they keep moving from place to place in search of customers. They deal in consumer goods of daily use, often of low value, and give time and place utility.
Peddlers and hawkers: carry goods on bicycles, handcarts, cycle-rickshaws or on their heads, and sell from place to place at the doorstep of customers, e.g. vegetables, fruits, snacks, toys.
Market traders: open shops at different places on fixed days or dates, e.g. weekly markets (haats) on Mondays in one place and Thursdays in another.

Street traders (pavement vendors): sell at places with huge floating population, such as near railway stations, bus stands and busy streets; they sell common-use items like stationery, eatables, newspapers and readymade garments.

Cheap jacks: have independent shops of a temporary nature in a business locality; they keep changing their location depending on the potential of the place, and deal in consumer items and repairs (e.g. watches, shoes, buckets).

example.q: Ramu sets up a temporary stall near a new housing colony to repair shoes and sell buckets. After three months he shifts to another locality with better business. What type of itinerant retailer is he?
steps: He has a temporary shop, not just a moving cart.
He shifts location according to business potential.
That describes a cheap jack.

learn.hook: The general store in your colony, the school-uniform shop near the bus stop and the second-hand bookshop near college: all are fixed-shop small retailers.
points: Fixed-shop retailers have permanent establishments to sell their goods; they have greater resources than itinerant retailers and offer more services like home delivery and credit.
General stores: located in residential areas, they stock a variety of products for daily needs, such as groceries, toiletries and stationery, and are open for long hours.
Speciality shops: sell a specific type of product within a line, e.g. only children's garments, men's wear, school uniforms or college books; they are usually in central locations.
Single line stores: sell a single product line but in a wide variety, e.g. readymade garments, watches, shoes, books, computers.

Street stall holders: small vendors at street crossings or busy places, selling cheap goods like hosiery, toys, soft drinks; they have a small fixed stall. Second-hand goods shops: sell used goods such as books, clothes, furniture and utensils at lower prices.

example.q: Classify: (a) a shop selling only school uniforms; (b) a shop selling all kinds of footwear; (c) a shop selling old furniture.
steps: (a) A specific type within the clothing line: speciality shop.
(b) One line (footwear) in many varieties: single line store.
(c) Used goods: second-hand goods shop.
example.answer: (a) Speciality shop, (b) single line store, (c) second-hand goods shop.

learn.hook: Clothes on the first floor, electronics on the second, a café on the third, all under one roof. That is the departmental store.
points: A departmental store is a large establishment offering a wide variety of products, classified into well-defined departments, aimed at satisfying practically every need of the customer under one roof. Each department specialises in one line.

Features: large size, usually centrally located; provides facilities like restaurants, travel bureaus, rest rooms and parking under one roof; combines retailing with warehousing; buys directly from manufacturers; centralised purchasing and decentralised sales across departments; often organised as a company with a board.

Merits: attracts a large number of customers due to central location; convenience in buying (all needs under one roof); attractive services; economy of large-scale operations; promotion of sales through advertising and display.

Limitations: lack of personal attention to customers; high operating cost (rent, staff, services), so prices tend to be high; high possibility of losses due to high costs and changing demand; inconvenient location for buyers who need something urgently, since it is usually in the city centre.

example.q: Mrs Iyer wants to buy a saree, a pressure cooker and a toy, and have lunch, without travelling to different shops. Which retail format suits her, and which merit does this show?
steps: She needs many types of goods plus food in one place.
A departmental store has many departments and services under one roof.
This shows the merit of convenience in buying.
example.answer: Departmental store; merit: convenience in buying.

topics.title: Chain stores (multiple shops) and comparison with departmental stores

learn.hook: The same shoe shop with the same look, same prices and same products in Pune, Patna and Puducherry: that is a chain store.
points: Chain stores or multiple shops are networks of retail shops owned and operated by manufacturers or intermediaries, located in different localities across the country, with similar appearance and dealing in standardised, branded products.

Features: located in fairly populous localities; manufacturing or purchasing is centralised at the head office; each shop is supervised by a branch manager; the head office controls policies; prices are fixed and all sales are on a cash basis; sales proceeds are deposited daily; dealing in a limited range of products.

Merits: economies of scale (central purchasing); elimination of middlemen; no bad debts (cash sales); transfer of goods from one branch to another; diffusion of risk (losses in one shop offset by profits in others); low cost of operation; flexibility (an unprofitable shop can be closed or shifted).

Limitations: limited selection of goods (only the firm's own range); lack of initiative (branch managers follow head office instructions); lack of personal touch; difficult to change products quickly when demand changes.

Departmental store vs chain store: one central location vs many localities near customers; wide variety of products vs limited range of a specific type; maximum services vs limited services; prices not uniform (discounts used to clear stock) vs uniform fixed prices; may give credit vs strictly cash; caters mostly to higher-income groups vs various income groups.

example.q: A shoe company has 400 shops across India. One shop in a small town keeps making losses. What can the company do, and which merits of chain stores does this show?
steps: It can close or shift the loss-making shop: flexibility.
Profits of the other shops cover this loss: diffusion of risk.
It can also move unsold stock to branches with higher demand.
example.answer: Close or shift the shop and move stock; shows flexibility, diffusion of risk and transfer of goods.

learn.reallife: Footwear, pharmacy and fashion chains with identical-looking outlets across Indian towns are classic multiple shops.

learn.hook: Long before apps, people in small towns ordered books, seeds and gadgets from catalogues and received them by post. That is mail order business.
points: Mail order houses are retail outlets that sell goods through mail. There is generally no direct personal contact between buyers and sellers.

Prospective customers are approached through advertisements in newspapers and magazines, circulars, catalogues, samples and price lists sent by post. Orders are received by mail, and goods are sent through the post office, often by VPP (value payable post), where the customer pays on delivery.
Suitable for: standardised and graded goods, which can be easily described; goods that can be transported easily at low cost; not suitable for perishable goods or goods requiring personal inspection.

Merits: limited capital requirement (no costly shop); elimination of middlemen; absence of bad debts (payment in advance or on delivery); wide reach (anywhere the post reaches); convenience (goods delivered at the doorstep).

Limitations: lack of personal contact; high promotion costs (advertising and catalogues); no after-sales services; no facility of credit; possibility of abuse (fraud by dishonest sellers); dependence on postal services.

example.q: A firm in Delhi sells standard-size calendars and diaries through catalogues sent by post and delivers them by VPP. Why are bad debts absent?
steps: Under VPP, the customer pays when the parcel is delivered.
The post office collects the money before handing over goods.
No goods are given on credit.
example.answer: Because payment is collected on delivery (VPP), so there is no credit and hence no bad debts.

learn.reallife: India Post's value payable post service made mail order business possible across small towns, and today's e-commerce is its digital descendant.

topics.title: Goods and Services Tax (GST): concept and structure

learn.hook: Before 2017, goods crossing state borders faced different taxes and long queues of trucks at check posts. GST changed this with 'One Nation, One Tax'.
points: Goods and Services Tax (GST) is a comprehensive, destination-based indirect tax levied on the supply of goods and services. It came into force on 1 July 2017 after the Constitution (101st Amendment) Act, 2016.

It replaced many central and state indirect taxes, such as central excise duty, service tax, VAT, central sales tax, entry tax, octroi and luxury tax. Destination-based means the tax revenue goes to the state where goods or services are consumed.

Intra-state supply (within the same state): Central GST (CGST) and State GST (SGST) are levied, shared equally; in Union Territories without their own legislature, UTGST replaces SGST. Example: at 18%, it is CGST 9% + SGST 9%.
Inter-state supply (from one state to another) and imports: Integrated GST (IGST) is levied by the Centre, and later shared with the destination state. Example: at 18%, IGST is 18%.
The GST Council, chaired by the Union Finance Minister and including state finance ministers, recommends GST rates, exemptions and rules.

example.q: A trader in Jaipur sells goods worth ₹50,000 at 18% GST (a) to a buyer in Jodhpur and (b) to a buyer in Pune. What taxes apply in each case?
steps: (a) Jaipur to Jodhpur is within Rajasthan: intra-state.
(b) Jaipur to Pune is from Rajasthan to Maharashtra: inter-state.

learn.reallife: After GST, many state-border check posts were removed, cutting the time trucks spend waiting on highways.

topics.title: Input tax credit, GSTN, composition scheme and chambers of commerce

learn.hook: Before GST, a shopkeeper often paid tax on tax: the tax already included in his purchase price was taxed again when he sold. Input tax credit fixed this.
points: Input tax credit (ITC): a registered business can deduct the GST it has already paid on purchases (input tax) from the GST it collects on sales (output tax), and pays only the difference. This removes the cascading effect (tax on tax).
GSTN (Goods and Services Tax Network) is the IT backbone of GST: it provides the online portal for registration, filing returns and paying tax for taxpayers, the Centre and states.

Registration: businesses whose aggregate turnover crosses a prescribed threshold must register. At present the threshold is ₹40 lakh a year for most suppliers of goods and ₹20 lakh for service providers, with lower limits in some special-category states; the government can revise it.

Composition scheme: an optional, simpler scheme for small taxpayers (turnover up to ₹1.5 crore for most traders and manufacturers), who pay tax at a low fixed rate on their turnover with fewer returns; they cannot claim input tax credit and cannot charge GST to their customers on their bills.

Chambers of commerce and industry, such as FICCI, CII and ASSOCHAM, promote internal trade by working with government on transportation and inter-state movement, harmonisation of taxes and levies, marketing of agro-products, weights and measures and prevention of duplicate brands, promoting sound infrastructure, and simplifying labour laws.

example.q: A manufacturer sells goods to a retailer for ₹10,000 + 18% GST. The retailer sells them for ₹15,000 + 18% GST. How much GST does the retailer pay to the government after input tax credit?
steps: Input tax (paid on purchase) = 18% of 10,000 = ₹1,800.
Output tax (collected on sale) = 18% of 15,000 = ₹2,700.
Net GST payable = 2,700 − 1,800 = ₹900.
This equals 18% of the value added (₹5,000).

learn.reallife: Every month lakhs of businesses file their GST returns online on the GST portal run by GSTN.
